https://www.budapesttimes.hu/hungary/gov.text: The Budapest Times Government pledges dialogue with Hungarians abroad at Petőfi memorial inauguration It is the duty of the Hungarian government to represent the rights of Hungarians living beyond the borders, which also means that these rights cannot be diminished, Zoltán Tarr, Minister for Social Relations and Culture, stressed on Sunday in Fehéregyháza, Transylvania, at the inauguration ceremony of the restored and expanded Petőfi memorial site. At the settlement near Segesvár, participants commemorated the 177th anniversary of the Battle of Fehéregyháza (also known as the Battle of Segesvár), which took place on 31 July 1849, and held the inauguration of the Petőfi memorial site — restored with Hungarian state support — along with the opening of the new permanent exhibition. The commemoration began with a festive church service at the Unitarian church, where Unitarian Bishop István Kovács led the prayer, followed by a sermon delivered by Reverend László Szabó. In his ceremonial address — his first visit to Transylvania as minister — Zoltán Tarr spoke about support policy and stated that the support provided by the motherland in previous years would be reviewed, and that in cases of abuse the necessary legal measures would be taken. According to the minister, the previous government used Hungarians living beyond the borders to extend its ideological and political influence. “We must ask for forgiveness — on their behalf too — from every deceived — forgive the expression — hoodwinked and fear-ridden compatriot living beyond the borders,” he said. “We ourselves promise our fellow citizens consultation and dialogue, conversations — because this is what there was no opportunity for over the past year,” he said. He added that it is his conviction that the parties, through conversation, can arrive at the common ground needed to make the Hungarian nation strong, brave, and hopeful once again. Speaking about the Battle of Fehéregyháza, which also resulted in the disappearance of Sándor Petőfi, he said that the Hungarian nation has been able to move beyond every oppressive regime and historical low point, and he believed that 2026 represents an opportunity for a new beginning for the Hungarian nation. Hungarian history contains countless periods that serve as reminders of how brave, free, and capable of anything for their homeland the Hungarians are, and this bravery and freedom is the shared national foundation that has held the nation together even in the most difficult of times — and it is from this that the future the current government wants to build also draws its strength, he said. He also touched on the fact that while many people know Sándor Petőfi, few truly know who he really was, and that the new permanent exhibition attempts to step away from the statue, from the cult author, and to rediscover the greatness and value of his life’s work through the lens of his disappearance and death. Hunor Kelemen, president of the Democratic Alliance of Hungarians in Romania (RMDSZ), expressed his gratitude to members of previous generations who had tended the Petőfi memorial site near Segesvár even when there were no resources to do so or when it was outright forbidden. In the case of Sándor Petőfi, there is a danger that the person disappears behind the cult, he suggested, and reminded those present that Hungary’s greatest poet wrote significant poems in Partium and Transylvania, and that the Petőfi cult also originated there. “It was in Transylvania that he found love, and it was here that he fell in battle for his other love — freedom,” he recalled. He warned that freedom remains fragile in the 21st century as well, and that its preservation always depends on the contemporary generation: it must be defended and passed on. Freedom is always a matter of decision, courage, and recognition, and the Hungarians of Transylvania choose it whenever they stand up for their rights, build institutions, and refuse to let others decide on their behalf. There is no freedom without human dignity, and where the freedom of the individual is diminished, so too is that of the community, he said. In Transylvania, freedom means living it not against others, but together with them, he stressed. According to Ferenc Péter, president of Mureș County Council — which maintains both the Mureș County Museum and the Fehéregyháza museum operating as one of its subsidiary units — the task of the Petőfi Museum is to authentically preserve the poet’s legacy and make it comprehensible to future generations. Its renovation is the result of cross-border cooperation, “because Petőfi’s legacy cannot be confined within administrative borders,” he said. According to Petra Török, director of the Petőfi Literary Museum, which participated in the project as a partner, the new permanent exhibition also pays tribute to those heroes “who were not given a grave in the nation’s cemetery.” She recalled the heroes who died in the battle near Segesvár and their widows, and spoke about how the exhibition also presents material relics uncovered on the former battlefield. https://telex.hu/belfold/2026/08/11/baka.text: Menü Kereső „Nem építhetjük az új Magyarországot a bosszúra” – videón Baka András első beszéde Belföld Baka András – Fotó: Máthé Zoltán / MTI Pál Tamás Állítsd be a Telexet megbízható forrásnak! Beállítom „Váratlan, zavarba ejtő és egyben megtisztelő volt már a jelölésem is” – mondta Baka András, miután az Országgyűlés keddi ülésén Magyarország köztársasági elnökévé választották . A Tisza Párt által jelölt Baka a köszöntő beszédében azt mondta, azért vállalta el a felkérést, mert úgy gondolja, hogy Magyarország olyan időszakhoz érkezett, amikor az állam működéséről, az alkotmányosságról és az ország közösségéről való komoly gondolkodásra van szükség. „Az elmúlt évek után a társadalom többsége most felszabadulást és reményt érez. Mások csalódottságot és bizonytalanságot. Ezek az érzések együtt vannak jelen a mai Magyarországon. Egy demokratikus társadalomban ez nem rendellenesség, hanem természetes állapot” – mondta Baka, majd hosszan sorolta az elmúlt 16 év hibáit. Az új köztársasági elnök szerint az új korszak kezdetén nem kerülhető el a szembenézés, mert tudnunk kell, hogy hogyan jutottunk idáig. Baka szerint egy generációnyi időt vesztegetett el Magyarország, miközben a rendszerváltozás éltanulójából a sereghajtó országok közé süllyedtünk. „Az elmúlt közel két évtizedben Magyarország olyan súlyos válságba került, amely a jogállam, a társadalom, a gazdaság, az államháztartás, az energiaellátás, a vízgazdálkodás, a környezetvédelem és a közlekedés területét egyaránt érinti” – mondta Baka. Kiemelte, hogy a magyar egészségügy, oktatás és gyermekvédelem régóta ismert tragikus helyzetben van, és arról is beszélt, hogy az elmúlt időszakban a közös javaink jelentős része magánérdekek szolgálatába került. Az elmúlt évek legnagyobb problémájának azonban a társadalom mély megosztottságát tartja. „Budapestet a vidékkel, fiatalt az időssel, hívőt a nem hívővel, jobboldalit a baloldalival, konzervatívot a liberálissal, kisebbséget a többséggel, gazdagot a szegénnyel, különböző társadalmi csoportokat egymással állították szembe” – mondta. Azt is megemlítette, hogy a közelmúltban civil szervezetek, újságírók, kisebbségek, külföldiek és másként gondolkodó polgárok váltak a gyűlöletkeltő politikai kampányok célpontjaivá. Baka András arra figyelmeztetett, hogy mindezen sérelmek ellenére egy dolgot biztosan nem tehetünk: „Nem építhetjük az új Magyarországot a bosszúra.” A Legfelsőbb Bíróság volt elnöke szerint a jogállam nem csak attól működik, hogy vannak szabályai, hanem attól is, hogy az emberek elhiszik, ezek a szabályok kivétel nélkül mindenkire vonatkoznak. „A jogsértéseket fel kell tárni, a közpénzek felhasználását ellenőrizni kell. Ahol a törvény megsértésének gyanúja fennáll, ott az állami szerveknek kötelességük eljárni, a bűnösséget pedig a bíróságoknak kell megállapítaniuk” – tette hozzá. Baka arról is beszélt, hogy a 2026-os választás megmutatta, hogy egy társadalom képes visszaszerezni az önrendelkezését, a következő évek kérdése pedig az lesz, hogy mit kezdünk ezzel a lehetőséggel. Szerinte súlyos tévedés volna azt gondolni, hogy egy választási eredmény önmagában helyreállítja a jogállamot. Úgy véli, olyan alkotmányos kultúrára van szükség Magyarországon, amelyben a hatalom korlátozása nem akadály, a politikai ellenfél nem ellenség, a kritika nem árulás, a kompromisszum pedig nem gyengeség. Baka a beszédében arra is kitért, hogy számára mit jelent a köztársasági elnöki intézmény. „A jelenlegi hatályos alaptörvény azt mondja, hogy a köztársasági elnök kifejezi a nemzet egységét, és őrködik az államszervezet demokratikus működése felett. Mit jelent számomra a nemzet egységének kifejezése? Mindenekelőtt pártpolitikai semlegességet, de semmiképpen sem jelent értéksemlegességet” – mondta. „Számomra a nemzet egysége nem azt jelenti, hogy mindannyian ugyanazt gondoljuk. Azt jelenti, hogy politikai és világnézeti különbségeinktől függetlenül mindannyian egyenlő méltósággal és jogokkal tartozunk ugyanahhoz a nemzethez. A magam részére meghatározónak tartom azt is, hogy a köztársaság elnöke az alkotmányos rend, az Európai Unió és a magyar nemzet történetileg kialakult alapértékeit kövesse és erősítse” – mondta az új államfő, aki azzal a gondolattal zárta a beszédét, hogy: „Az állam nem önmagáért van, az állam az emberért van.” A 73 éves jogtudós Baka Andrást 140 igennel, 6 nemmel, 0 tartózkodással titkos szavazáson választották meg kedden a következő köztársasági elnöknek. Hivatalosan augusztus 19-én lép hivatalba. A Fidesz és a KDNP képviselői nem vettek részt a megválasztásában. Kedvenceink Partnereinktől Állítsd be a Telexet megbízható forrásnak! Photograph: Apu Gomes/AFP/Getty Images Los Angeles LA homelessness non-profit workers arrested over alleged corruption and bribes Pair accused of misappropriating millions in taxpayer dollars as Trump officials target alleged fraud in blue states Cecilia Nowell Wed 16 Sep 2026 19.34 EDT First published on Wed 16 Sep 2026 17.13 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Federal law enforcement officers have arrested two employees of California-based homelessness non-profits on corruption charges, alleging that they misappropriated millions in taxpayer dollars. The US justice department has arrested Michael Young, a founder of the Culver City-based nonprofit Home At Last, and Lakiya Malone, an employee of the Los Angeles-based Special Service for Groups. The two are expected to appear in court on Wednesday. Young is charged with wire fraud in a scheme to embezzle more than $7.5m from contracts with Los Angeles county and other publicly funded agencies, which he used to open a high-end restaurant, nightclub and bingo hall. Malone is charged with taking more than $180,000 in bribes and kickbacks from the director of another homelessness non-profit, Alexander Soofer, who has agreed to plead guilty in a separate case. The justice department is also seeking to arrest Donye Mitchell, the CEO of the Los Angeles-based nonprofit The Big Blue Umbrella. Mitchell is charged with wire fraud in a case that alleges he fraudulently obtained $1.2m in public grant funding, which he allegedly used for personal expenses, including his own bail bonds, credit card debt and PlayStation charges “My message to every fraudster who steals from the vulnerable is clear: we will track you down, bring charges where the evidence leads, and work relentlessly to reclaim every taxpayer dollar you stole,” said assistant attorney general Colin M McDonald of the National Fraud Enforcement Division. The investigation was led by the homeless fraud and corruption taskforce, which US attorney Bill Essayli formed last year to “investigate fraud, waste, abuse, and corruption involving funds allocated toward the eradication of homelessness within the seven-county jurisdiction of the central district of California”. Los Angeles mayor Karen Bass said in a Wednesday statement: “My administration has zero tolerance for fraud – period. “Any misuse of taxpayer funds meant to help unhoused Angelenos should be met with the full force of the law. We appreciate the efforts of the Department of Justice in protecting public funds and working towards recovering dollars meant to serve Angelenos experiencing homelessness.” The arrests come amid growing Trump administration-backed efforts to root out “fraud” in blue states, such as California . In April, Donald Trump named JD Vance his “fraud czar” , with a focus on investigating “those blue states where crooked Democrat politicians … have had a ‘free for all’ in the unprecedented theft of taxpayer money”. Months prior, he froze federal childcare funding to Minnesota over accusations of such fraud, and halted more than a quarter-billion dollars in Medicaid funds to the state as part of efforts to ensure it was a “good steward of the American people’s tax money”. This summer, the Trump administration suspended federal funding to Los Angeles’s homelessness agency, Lahsa, pending an investigation citing allegations of fraud. At the time, about 8% of Lahsa’s budget came from federal funding. And earlier this week, 12 people in southern California were charged with fraudulently collecting $10m in government childcare payments, despite allegedly caring for few or no children. “If you fail the taxpayer, if you fail our cities, if you fail our shared mission of ending homelessness, there will be consequences and we will cut you off,” housing and urban development secretary Scott Turner said at a press conference. https://www.designboom.com/design/latern.text: readers submit now competitions open call events promote courses teach it design-directory get listed shop start selling milan.design.week venice.arch.biennale venice.art.biennale get more from designboom bookmark and build your own library full overview of your project submissions first to know about announcements more to come sign in create a free account not now [FEATURED] Laterna Magika made the screen part of the stage Developed by stage director Alfréd Radok and scenographer Josef Svoboda for Czechoslovakia’s pavilion at Expo 58 in Brussels, Laterna Magika brought live performance, film projection, music, dance and stage technology into a single theatrical language, turning the relationship between the physical stage and the projected image into the central subject of the performance. The project continued beyond the exhibition, becoming an independent company of Prague’s National Theatre in 1959, developing a theatrical language that still offers a useful way of thinking about spectatorship, scenography and the way projected images can alter our experience of physical space. The idea that a filmed image could interact with a performer on stage as if they occupied the same world shaped Laterna Magika. In the original Expo program, filmed figures appeared to speak to the actress performing live, while projected sequences were carefully timed with acting, music and dance. The screen became part of the action, giving the audience something else to follow alongside the performers in front of them. An image could respond to a performer, extend a movement or introduce another version of the same space, while the physical stage remained visible at the same time. For the audience, watching the performance meant moving between different layers, paying attention to what was happening in front of them and to what was happening on screen. Looking at Laterna Magika today, this way of working feels particularly relevant because screens have become part of so many physical environments, from theaters and museums to public spaces and buildings. Svoboda and Radok were already exploring what happens when an image is given a physical role within a space, and when the audience has to consider the performer and their projected image as two parts of the same scene. all images courtesy of Josef Svoboda josef svoboda and the architecture of the image Josef Svoboda worked at Prague’s National Theatre from the late 1940s and became head of its artistic-technical operations, where he pushed the theater workshops toward a more technologically ambitious model capable of responding to increasingly complex stage designs. His approach treated light, projection, movement and technical infrastructure as active components of the stage environment. His work with Alfréd Radok at Expo 58 grew out of this broader interest in expanding what scenography could do. The two developed an interplay between live action and filmed sequences in which the projected image could heighten or contradict what was happening on stage, producing a visual language that depended on precise timing and coordination between different media. The National Theatre later described Laterna Magika as having evolved from these principles, with each production exploring a different way of connecting stage and image. Svoboda’s thinking also extended into the technical systems that made these relationships possible. His work on Polyekran, which involved combining multiple projection surfaces into a larger image composition, was developed around the same period, although the National Theatre makes an important distinction between Polyekran as a technical system and Laterna Magika as a theatrical form. Both belonged to Svoboda’s broader investigation into how projected images could alter the perception of space. dancers perform on a raised platform beneath a large projected eye a theater built around spectatorship Seen through contemporary scenography, Laterna Magika belongs to a longer history of treating the stage as a space that can direct and shape attention. The audience moves between what is physically present and what appears on screen, following performers, images, light and movement as they occupy and alter the same space. In this sense, Laterna Magika changes the role of the spectator, who has to follow both the performer and the projected image and understand how the two relate to each other. The stage becomes something that has to be read as much as watched, with projection, movement, light and physical space working together to determine what the audience sees. three illuminated stage structures carry projected figures in a Laterna Magika performance from expo spectacle to an evolving theater The original program was designed for an international exhibition and carried the representational ambitions that came with that context, yet its theatrical language continued after Expo 58. Laterna Magika became an independent company of the National Theatre in Prague in May 1959, initially continuing with revue-like programs before gradually developing longer productions and a broader theatrical repertoire. One of its most enduring productions, Wonderful Circus, premiered in 1977 and remains in the repertoire. Its arrival marked a shift toward multi-theme productions, while the company continued to develop the relationship between live performers and projected imagery as a defining part of its stage language. Svoboda became Laterna Magika’s artistic director in 1973, at a moment when the company was searching for a new direction, and remained closely connected to its development for the rest of his career. His influence also extended beyond individual productions into the question of where this kind of theater should exist: during the development of Prague’s New Stage in the early 1980s, he pushed for the building to accommodate Laterna Magika, helping reshape the project around the needs of the company. The New Stage opened in 1983 and became closely associated with Laterna Magika, giving the company a permanent architectural setting for a theatrical form that had originally been conceived for a temporary exhibition. This particular form of scenography helped generate the architectural conditions in which it could continue to develop. a dancer performs against fragmented projections that extend across the stage the stage after the stage Looking at Laterna Magika today makes sense because so much of contemporary performance is once again concerned with the relationship between the physical and the projected image. Projection, LED screens, virtual production and responsive lighting are now part of the visual language of theaters, exhibitions and architecture, making Svoboda and Radok’s experiments feel less like an isolated moment in theater history and more like an earlier chapter in a conversation that is still taking place. What is striking is how much of that conversation was already present in Laterna Magika. The technology has changed, but the basic setup remains recognizable: a performer shares the stage with an image, the image changes our perception of the space, and the audience has to decide how to look at both at the same time. Looking back at the work now allows us to see where some of these ideas came from, before projection became such a familiar part of the environments we move through today. This is also what makes Svoboda’s approach to scenography worth revisiting. He treated the stage as something that could change through light, movement, projection and technology, giving the image a physical presence within the performance. At a moment when screens are increasingly built into the spaces around us, Laterna Magika offers a useful point of reference for understanding how that relationship between image, space and the spectator developed in the first place. a dancer performs beside a projected silhouette within a circular frame performers gather around a suspended stage structure as projected shadows fill the backdrop the imagery extends across the stage behind the performers a live performer appears alongside a large projected image of two faces performers occupy separate pools of light beneath a large circular projection live performers appear in front of large-scale projections of circus characters and scenes a performer stands in front of a projected vintage car, combining live action with film imagery projected imagery surrounds two performers on stage projected musicians appear behind a live pianist and performer an audience watches a large-scale projected image made up of multiple screen panels Polyekran involved combining multiple projection surfaces into a larger image composition This article is part of designboom’s SPECTATOR AND SPECTACLE chapter, asking how wonder gets built, and how it might return some mystery to a world that has measured most of it away.
